content:
Sometimes Lean is unnecessarily unfolding instances in typeclass search. Here is an example.

class A (X : Type) where
  a : Nat
  ab : Nat

class B (X : Type) where
  b : Nat
  ab : Nat

class AB (X : Type) extends A X, B X where

instance Empty.instAB : AB Empty where
  a := 0
  b := 0
  ab := 0

class D (X : Type) extends AB X where

instance Empty.instD : D Empty where

example : Empty.instD.toAB = Empty.instAB := by with_reducible_and_instances rfl

example : Empty.instD.toAB.toB = Empty.instAB.toB := by with_reducible_and_instances rfl

A X and B X are typeclasses with an overlapping field ab. The typeclass AB X extends both, and D X extends AB X. The type Empty has instances of both AB and D and there is no diamond; both examples work. The first example says that the D instance, restricted to AB, equals the AB instance. The second says that the D and AB instances, restricted to B, are equal. No surprises there.

The surprise, for me, is in the typeclass trace for the rfls, which I have completely unfolded for both examples in the spoiler below.

Typeclass trace

example : Empty.instD.toAB = Empty.instAB := by with_reducible_and_instances rfl
/-
  [definition.value] [5886.000000] ✅️ _example ▼
...
                  [Meta.isDefEq] [308.000000] ✅️ Empty.instD.toAB =?= Empty.instAB ▼
                    [whnf] [90.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: Empty.instD ▼
                      [] [18.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: { toAB := Empty.instAB }
                    [] [6.000000] ✅️ Empty.instAB =?= Empty.instAB -/

example : Empty.instD.toAB.toB = Empty.instAB.toB := by with_reducible_and_instances rfl
/-
  [definition.value] [7558.000000] ✅️ _example ▼
...
                  [Meta.isDefEq] [2065.000000] ✅️ Empty.instD.toB =?= Empty.instAB.toB ▼
                    [] [1822.000000] ✅️ { b := AB.b Empty, ab := A.ab Empty } =?= { b := AB.b Empty, ab := A.ab Empty } ▼
                      [] [535.000000] ✅️ AB.b Empty =?= AB.b Empty ▼
                        [] [5.000000] ✅️ Empty =?= Empty
->                      [] [308.000000] ✅️ Empty.instD.toAB =?= Empty.instAB ▼
->                        [whnf] [90.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: Empty.instD ▼
->                          [] [18.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: { toAB := Empty.instAB }
->                        [] [6.000000] ✅️ Empty.instAB =?= Empty.instAB
                      [] [1058.000000] ✅️ A.ab Empty =?= A.ab Empty ▼
                        [] [5.000000] ✅️ Empty =?= Empty
                        [] [834.000000] ✅️ Empty.instD.toA =?= Empty.instAB.toA ▼
                          [] [604.000000] ✅️ Empty.instD.toAB.1 =?= Empty.instAB.1 ▼
                            [whnf] [14.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: AB Empty
                            [whnf] [300.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: Empty.instD.toAB ▼
                              [] [211.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: Empty.instD.1 ▼
                                [] [87.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: Empty.instD ▼
                                  [] [17.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: { toAB := Empty.instAB }
                                [] [17.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: { a := 0, ab := 0, b := 0 }
                            [whnf] [39.000000] ✅️ Non-easy whnf: Empty.instAB
                            [] [5.000000] ✅️ { a := 0, ab := 0 } =?= { a := 0, ab := 0 }
                      [] [5.000000] ✅️ Empty =?= Empty

-/

The first example (equality on AB) is quick. Lean is quick to spot that Empty.instD.toAB = Empty.instAB, doesn't unfold anything any further, and we're done in 308 mHeartbeats. The second defeq check takes seven times as long! Why?

Even though Lean is capable of proving (without unfolding) that these two AB instances are equal, when asked to check that their projections down to B are equal Lean decides to unfold them both. The resulting trace looks very inefficient (to me). First Lean unfolds both instances to see the b and ab fields. Then Lean tries to check that the b fields are equal, and to do this it checks that Empty.instD.toAB = Empty.instAB. In particular it has to check equality of these two AB instances anyway (which it does in 308 mHeartbeats just as in the first example -- I flagged the calculation with -> in the trace). Then it checks that the ab fields are equal (even though this can be deduced from the fact that the AB instances are equal, which it has already checked) and to do this it has to unfold all the way down to A, because A is the "preferred parent" of AB.

What I want to point out is: the current algorithm to check Empty.instD.toAB.toB = Empty.instAB.toB seems to be doomed to also check that Empty.instD.toAB = Empty.instAB, so it's going to do this anyway -- so why doesn't it only do that, because if i1 and i2 are equal then i1.toB and i2.toB are going to be equal as well. Furthermore, if the typeclass system is not being abused, then whenever Lean is being asked to prove i1.toB = i2.toB then it should expect that i1 = i2 is going to be true anyway. So why not cut this corner?

Background: I noticed this when trying to debug how making a type synonym into a one-field structure caused a surprising slowdown in FLT. What was happening was that checking equality of two fields of a class on this structure had now become slightly more costly, but the surprising thing was that the number of times these fields were being checked was huge -- far more than I had expected. In mathlib we have these tricks like fast_instance% which are used to attempt to make instances of classes in exactly the way that core wants so that the core algorithms are as fast as possible and we can avoid unfolding as much as possible. However because our algebra hierarchy is absolutely massive it is impossible to avoid situations such as the A,B,AB,D one above; in my case AB was Ring which has many data fields and B was AddGroupWithOne, not a "preferred parent", meaning that even though two Ring instances on WithVal K v were trivially defeq, it was taking a million mHeartbeats to verify that the corresponding AddGroupWithOne instances were defeq, and this was happening everywhere (in every line of every proof; even intro would take many heartbeats).

Furthermore, if the typeclass system is not being abused, then whenever Lean is being asked to prove i1.toB = i2.toB then it should expect that i1 = i2 is going to be true anyway. So why not cut this corner?

Is this necessarily true? It seems reasonable to me that you could have two distinct types i1 ≠ i2 which coerce to some weaker type i1.toB = i2.toB which are defeq. Like, for example couldn't you have two distinct Ring structures which both reduce to the same AddCommGroup via Ring.toAddCommGroup?

What I want to point out is: the current algorithm to check Empty.instD.toAB.toB = Empty.instAB.toB seems to be doomed to also check that Empty.instD.toAB = Empty.instAB, so it's going to do this anyway -- so why doesn't it only do that, because if i1 and i2 are equal then i1.toB and i2.toB are going to be equal as well.

I do agree that this would be a very good optimization for typeclass inference. It should at least try to prove i1 = i2 before unfolding the full definitions for i1.toB and i2.toB.

Jack McCarthy said:

Is this necessarily true? It seems reasonable to me that you could have two distinct types i1 ≠ i2 which coerce to some weaker type i1.toB = i2.toB which are defeq. Like, for example couldn't you have two distinct Ring structures which both reduce to the same AddCommGroup via Ring.toAddCommGroup?

This is exactly the kind of abuse of the typeclass system that Kevin is assuming doesn't happen, right? The assumption is that there will only be up to one instance of each typeclass on a given type.
Ah I see, I didn't realize that was considered to be typeclass abuse

Just a random story related to this: over the weekend, despite knowing essentially nothing about Exprs/metaprogramming etc, I used Claude to edit Lean's typeclass inference algorithm, rebuild lean and mathlib, and then compare and contrast. I didn't even have to learn how to compile Lean, indeed I didn't even have to learn how to do anything, the AI did it all. To my astonishment and delight Lean compiled first time, all the tests passed, and mathlib nearly compiled, but one declaration started timing out. My edits (Claude's edits) were an attempt to experiment with and understand the issue I raised above, which of course is the best way to learn.

The issue above shows that in some cases, typeclass inference is slower than it could be, when it succeeds. My edit makes it quicker when it succeeds but slower when it fails (surprise surprise, it's swings and roundabouts). But typeclass inference fails a lot in mathlib. The experiment flagged various declarations in mathlib where fishy typeclass inference things were going on (failures which shouldn't be failing and which can be helped along with more elaboration). In short: I have learnt more about mathlib as a result of this experiment, which a year or two ago would I think have been completely impossible to do. Exciting times!

(You'll note that the lean4 repo has a .claude directory, with some lean4 specific advice to AIs building and testing lean. It's mostly just Claude here, but making the repo friendly to Claude in this way definitely helps, too.)

So in fact I got sucked into this. When I posted the message at the top of this thread about a month ago, I basically meant "I can see a possible win here (with my naive eyes) but it would involve changing the typeclass inference system which obviously I can't do". What I realised yesterday is that actually there's nothing stopping me from changing the typeclass inference system other than a payment of $20 which has enabled me to do 5 or so experiments over a 2 day period (occasionally waiting for claude to recharge), from "solve all instance defeq problems of the form f i1 =?= f i2 by first trying to solve i1 =?= i2 and then going back to the old algorithm" to "solve all instance defeq problems of the form f i1 =?= f i2 by first trying to solve i1 =?= i2 and then giving up if this fails" to "solve defeq problems of the form f i1 =?= f i2 when f is a certain kind of projection by first solving i1 =?= i2"etc etc. For each experiment I built lean and mathlib, or at least I tried to. Lean and >= 99% of the tests built almost every time. For three of the experiments mathlib didn't finish building, and for the other two mathlib did build but it was no faster than vanilla lean.

One thing I learnt, which probably experts knew already and indeed I think I've read before on this Zulip, is that mathlib basically expands to fill the space provided. If you try to make a core change which makes some theoretical things not work which used to work, then mathlib will not work because those theoretical things will be there. And if you try to make a core change which makes some things work quicker and other things work slower (for example, if you try to ensure that successful inference problems succeed more quickly but pay the cost that failures may fail more slowly) then mathlib might well get slower, because mathlib has optimised for the algorithm as it is, so gains are typically minimal but losses are painful.

The experiment also brought to light examples of typeclass inference in mathlib really going off the rails in places (because the changes I made almost always made typeclass failures be more costly, so things which were already slow would start timing out). For example docs#Field.toEuclideanDomain goes on a doomed search for [Meta.isDefEq] [4430725.000000] ❌️ ?a / 0 =?= a / 0 ▶ where the LHS has got an ?inst✝ : EuclideanDomain K embedded deep in it, which will never be found (it's what we're trying to prove) and then to rub salt into the wound it next goes on a search for [Meta.isDefEq] [4427499.000000] ❌️ ?a / 0 =?= 0 / 0 ▶ which is doomed for the same reason. Those failures contribute to 80% of the total time of elaboration of the declaration's value. I wish I understood the typeclass inference algorithm well enough to see why this is happening. The algorithm is something I've become forced to be interested in because I spend a lot of my time doing algebra when I'm doing Lean, and the algebra hierarchy is now a gigantic and extraordinary thing.

Another failing-in-one-of-my-patches declaration was docs#LaurentSeries.valuation_compare where typeclass inference fails expensively on master (and times out on one of my patches) because of some missing instances; I added them in #39186 , giving a 12% speedup in the file (and making it compile in the patch).

Other compilation failures were instances of "defeq abuse". I realised during the experiment that in some sense I was changing the definition of defeq (in the sense that I was changing the definition of isExprDefEqAuxImpl) so I was changing the definition of defeq abuse as well. It made me understand better that the concept of defeq is simply just an algorithm and that instead of trying to understand its meaning, you just have to understand the algorithm.

I'm out of credits now until Thursday, so I have to stop! But I found this experiment very educational and hope to think of other such experiments in the future. The tl;dr really is just that you can actually made edits to core Lean and see their effects on mathlib yourself, even if you know no metaprogramming, although it definitely helps to have a Claude subscription and a machine capable of running two instances of mathlib at once (so you can compare and contrast vanilla and the patch) (and ideally two monitors as well, so you can have one on each). Claude was also very good at reading instance traces by the way, but not perfect: it helped that I knew my way around instance traces already. But that's just an example of a more general phenomenon that you'll get more out of a language model if you're asking it questions in an area where you already know a lot.
I guess your issue is lean4#13063. Can you give the example to Claude and ask if it can solve it?
Exciting! All this seems worth a Xena post with more details and sharing of what you learnt.. :stuck_out_tongue:
